events.excerpt: NCCL 2.32.3 added TLS 1.3 PSK encryption of its TCP sockets via the process-global ncclSetEncryption . PyTorch has no way to enable it. Adds ProcessGroupNCCL.Options.encryption_psk , honored by nccl2 (which shares the Options class); legacy ProcessGroupNCCL (including shrink) rejects it and torchcomms (including split) raises instead of silently ignoring it. NCCL rereads the key for every new socket, including live communicators', so nccl2 applies it once in the constructor of the first group: later groups (including split children) must pass the same key or none, and a different key or a key on a non-first group raises. Mismatched keys across ranks can hang, as NCCL drops failed handshakes. NCCL validates length (>= 32 bytes); NUL bytes raise ValueError. NCCL < 2.32.3 and ROCm raise. NCCL builds without TLS (PyPI wheels, CI) accept the key and fail at communicator init. split / shrink children inherit the key; if a child can't apply its key, the already-created child comm is aborted and the error raised (validation can't precede the collective without hanging other ranks). Groups constructed with a key must not be constructed concurrently with other groups (documented, no new lock). events.excerpt: There are a lot of things you can do with an Xserver, but run it on a microcontroller? Well, if that microcontroller is an ESP32-S3, [Sergey Zorin]– and Claude– have got you covered with Woodland X11 , a full-featured port of everyone’s favourite XServer. Now, it is just the core Xserver with no extensions, and currently targeted specifically at the Elecrow CrowPanel Advance 4.3″, a device that packages an ESP32-S3-N16R8 with an 800×480 RGB565 IPS panel and GT911 touch. In this implementation, your finger is the Xcursor. There’s even two-finger scroll implemented, though no keyboard. As you can see in the demo video embedded below, it works well enough for those oldschool X applications like xclock, xcalc and– crucially!– xeyes. What’s the point of an Xserver without googly eyes, anyway? In reality, you’re not likely to set this up just for Xeyes, but the idea of having bringing Linux applications to a little display via WiFi or — as in the video– wired connection has no limit of use cases. Try that with Wayland ! Considering X11’s vintage, it is perhaps not surprising that it fits on the ESP32-S3, a chip we’ve seen emulate an entire 386 PC before– a PC that could run an Xserver, for you youngun’s. Thanks to [Sergey] for the tip!

events.excerpt: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006). events.excerpt: One of the struggles with vintage computer systems is that many of the ICs in them have no modern-day version that you can just purchase and drop-in. Creating replacements that use modern-day ICs inside has consequently become a popular direction, with [Philip Smart]’s TranZPUter being one such example . Standing for ‘transformable ZPU Computer’, the tranZPUter is transformable in the sense that it features an FPGA or MCU and the initial iteration targeting the ZPU Evo CPU design. This has led to a number of variants of this concept, including a version targeting the Z80 , the 6502 and 6809. These are based around the RP2350B MCU, using its PIO peripheral to great effect. Of these the Motorola 6809 is probably the lesser known MPU, having been launched in 1978 as an 8-bit MPU with some 16-bit features that could beat the 6502 in many metrics courtesy of its more advanced hardware. It being more expensive led to it only being used in systems like the TRS-80 Color, Dragon 32/64, SuperPET and a whole range of arcade systems. If you have any of those 6809-based systems and the MPU gave up the ghost, you can drop in the Pico6809 board featuring said RP2350B MCU as well as an ESP32 co-processor. events.excerpt: People often say that one day data will live on chain. Here is a case where it already does, and where the main result of using a blockchain is not financial. Since 28 September, when Robonomics moved to Polkadot, the record lives on Polkadot. As expected, the red wave has weighed on community sentiment, and the popular BTC Fear and Greed Index entered “extreme fear” territory. This may sound scary at first sight, but can it actually be good news? Darkest Before the Dawn? US inflation came in higher than expected, giving the Fed a solid reason to increase interest rates next month. Nvidia’s shares nosedived after its longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned amid an extramarital affairs scandal, triggering a broader sell-off across tech and crypto markets. These are some of the negative headlines that have rattled BTC and the altcoins over the past few days. And since crypto market behavior is very emotional, so are the participants in it.
